The brown greater galago (Otolemur crassicaudatus) is the largest member of the Galagidae family, a fact reflected in its substantial adult body size. Field surveys of wild populations consistently report that individuals attain a maximum body length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters], although considerable geographic variation is evident. In a detailed morphometric study across the species' southern African range, adult head-body lengths were found to range from 297 to 373 millimeters [Li = 297 to 373 millimeters], with larger specimens typically inhabiting more productive coastal forests. Neonates emerge after a gestation period of 130 days [tg = 130 days], a duration that unfolds under the species' typical core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This relatively long gestational investment, comparable to that of other strepsirrhines of similar mass, produces a single newborn weighing approximately 43.2 grams [Wwb = approximately 43.2 grams]. The altricial condition of the newborn, though evident in its closed eyes and limited mobility, is nevertheless accompanied by a firm grip that allows the infant to cling to the mother's fur shortly after delivery. At the species' typical core temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], complete nutritional independence from maternal milk is achieved at 138 days after birth [tx = 138 days after birth] and the weanling has reached a wet weight of 500 grams [Wwx = 500 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase from its birth mass.

Growth continues steadily through the juvenile and sub-adult phases, culminating in an ultimate wet weight of 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams] for fully grown adults. This asymptotic body mass places Otolemur crassicaudatus at the upper extreme of galagid size, exceeding its congener Otolemur garnettii by nearly a factor of two. The dietary transition from maternal milk to solid food begins gradually around the sixth week after birth, with the suckling juvenile initially consuming soft fruits and gums gathered by the mother. Under the stable thermal conditions provided by the mother's body at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the offspring's own thermoregulatory capacities develop progressively, allowing it to venture away from the maternal nest for increasingly extended foraging bouts before reaching the age of weaning. The substantial investment in each offspring, evident in the 500 grams [Wwx = 500 grams] mass at nutritional independence, reflects a life-history strategy characterized by high parental investment per capita and relatively low litter size, a pattern typical of many arboreal primates inhabiting resource-predictable environments where juvenile survival is strongly dependent on body condition entering the first dry season.

The pace of life for this large galago is leisurely relative to many other nocturnal primates, with maximum lifespan in captivity reaching 22.7 years [am = 22.7 years] at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This remarkable longevity is among the highest documented for any strepsirrhine primate and is comparable to that of cathemeral lemurs of considerably larger body size. Field-based mark-recapture studies in the iSimangaliso Wetland Park of South Africa have recovered individuals known to be at least 15 years of age, suggesting that the maximum longevity of 22.7 years [am = 22.7 years] observed in zoo-housed animals is not an artifact of captive care but rather reflects a genuine life-history capacity of the species at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Such extended lifespan is energetically underpinned by a diet dominated by exudates and fruits, which provides a relatively constant energy supply year-round, buffering the animals against seasonal food shortages that accelerate senescence in more specialized feeders. The species' low adult mortality rate, estimated from longitudinal studies, further corroborates the interpretation that Otolemur crassicaudatus follows a slow life-history trajectory, with individuals investing heavily in somatic maintenance and survival across many years.

At the species' regulated body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], reproductive maturation follows a sexually dimorphic schedule. Females experience the onset of puberty at 495 days after birth [tp = 495 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Males, by contrast, require a considerably longer developmental period, attaining sexual maturity at 639 days after birth [tp = 639 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This pronounced sexual bimaturism, in which males take approximately 30 percent longer than females to become reproductively competent, is thought to reflect the competitive demands of a polygynous mating system. Males must achieve not only somatic maturity but also the social and physical condition necessary to establish and defend access to receptive females. In captivity, the first behavioral signs of estrus in females precede actual conception by several weeks, and once mated, the gravid female enters a gestation that, at 130 days [tg = 130 days], represents a substantial fraction of her total reproductive cycle at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. The total energetic cost of producing and rearing a single offspring, from conception through the 138 days to weaning [tx = 138 days to weaning], is considerable for a 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams] adult female at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C].

Reproductive output in the brown greater galago is modest, consistent with its slow life history. Females typically give birth to a single infant per litter, with twinning being exceptionally rare in both wild and captive settings. At the species' typical core temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females produce approximately 1.5 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters annually], with each litter containing one offspring [N_R_i = each litter containing one offspring], yielding a maximum daily reproduction rate of 0.0041 offspring per day [Ri = 0.0041 offspring per day] relative to other mammals of comparable body size. The interbirth interval of roughly 8 months allows females sufficient time to recover somatic condition between successive reproductive events. The relatively extended period from birth to weaning, 138 days after birth [tx = 138 days after birth], ensures that the single offspring is nutritionally emancipated at a body mass of 500 grams [Wwx = 500 grams], a threshold below which post-weaning survival in the wild drops markedly at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Comparative data from other galagid species indicate that Otolemur crassicaudatus occupies the slow end of the reproductive spectrum, investing each offspring's complete growth trajectory—from the 43.2 grams [Wwb = 43.2 grams] neonate through the 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams] adult weight—over a lifespan that may extend to 22.7 years [am = 22.7 years] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C].
